speakers: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
summary: Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor 321 (Nov 2024, post US election): Alan Dunne and Niels on the Trump win (polls missed, inflation theme), the macro outlook (solid US growth, supply-side optimism, tariffs as bargaining chip, deficit/bond-yield risk), October's poor trend-following month (all three financial sectors reversed), a buffer-ETF question, Goldman's 3% 10-year S&P forecast and concentration, and the Invesco systematic investing survey.

coverage.note: Intro; European car industry and German government crisis
Europe competitiveness, demographics, policy paralysis; bearish on Europe; Don 50th anniversary
Election analysis: magnitude of win, polls underestimate, inflation theme, incumbents voted out
Niels thoughts: legal problems, inflation cause, podcasts, Musk, tariffs
Podcasts/Twitter, Musk, tariffs as bargaining chip, Bessent shadow Fed chair
US macro: recession risk faded, labour market, solid consumption, inflation, China policy
Asset market pattern, Trump policy expectations, tariffs one-off effect, supply-side optimism
Two years of control, deficit and bond yields rising since Fed cut, Bessent, deficit consensus
Own goal in yields, Fed pace revised, predictability, Greenspan-Clinton, deficits resolution; trend update intro
October trend-following loss: three financial sectors reversed, medium lookbacks, bond transitions
Trend index numbers; buffer ETF question and answer
Buffer ETFs vs trend, short duration; Goldman 10-year S&P forecast
Goldman concentration effect, forecasting swing variables, Alan view on yields and valuations
Discussion of concentration puzzle, rates and equities, trend followers do not predict, earnings vs valuations
Bond vs equity forecast, trend expected return, hard to sell alternatives; Invesco survey adoption stats
Invesco survey multi-asset systematic and AI usage; power of being systematic; mystery paper intro
Mystery paper: adding alternatives that trade held assets; outro

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: we've got this um challenge in Europe from the influx of EVS in particular from from from China
claims.claim: European autos (14 million jobs) face structural pressure from Chinese EV imports, shown by Volkswagen plant closure and pay-cut proposals.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: Rising debt levels and fiscal consolidation and and the tough choices that that have to be made in Europe amid a backdrop of you know growth in the German economy that's been pretty flat
claims.claim: The German coalition split over budget cuts reflects Europe's rising debt, flat growth and competitiveness challenges.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: it's hard to make the uh the bullish case on Europe as far as I can see at the moment
claims.claim: Europe's bullish case is hard to make: policy paralysis, aging population, immigration reluctance and no tech leaders hurt productivity.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: all this EU bureaucracy that we have trying to always have 27 countries kind of agree on things
claims.claim: EU bureaucracy of 27 countries slows decisions and hurts competitiveness, so Europe is falling behind.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: these Cycles are are long-term Cycles
claims.claim: Country relative economic strength moves in long cycles (Germany once far ahead, now Ireland has fiscal surpluses and full employment).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: what what has really surprised the markets I think is is the magnitude of the win and and the fact that it's a clean sweep
claims.claim: The Trump win was expected (55-66% in betting markets) but the clean sweep of both houses was the surprise.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: the polls uh underestimated uh Trump's uh support
claims.claim: Polls again underestimated Trump support, including final-weekend swing-state polls close or tied, with narratives bending to fit each data point.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: there's always a narrative um to to to fit whatever piece of data has been put forward
claims.claim: Narratives are constructed to fit any data point; post-hoc explanations are easy.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: High inflation and particularly grocery food prices that's really been the theme
claims.claim: High inflation (especially grocery prices) dominated the election even with full employment and record stocks.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: across the world we're seeing a general trend of you know governments being voted out after a term
claims.claim: Incumbent governments are being voted out worldwide after one term, a post-inflation pattern.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: you looked at all the legal problems he was facing you would think it's very unlikely that he's going to win the presidency and and and he does it
claims.claim: Low-probability outcomes occur; forecasts built on apparent obstacles can fail.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: inflation was caused probably from covid to to a large extent
claims.claim: Inflation was largely a COVID-era shock not rebutted in the campaign, partly worsened by Fed mistakes.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: I think I think it's it's it's more the latter
claims.claim: Tariffs are more a bargaining chip than an end game, though they cannot be ruled out as permanent.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: he also came up with this idea of the Shadow uh Fed chair
claims.claim: Bessent's shadow Fed chair idea could undermine the Fed's independence.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: the US um recession risk was was much more elevated it was starting to diminish and probably reaches a peak kind of in in in August
claims.claim: US recession risk peaked in August 2024 and faded, but Fed easing was delivered in September.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: if if corporates for whatever reason dramatically uh you know slowed in hiring and started to lay off people then that would lead into weaker consumption
claims.claim: The labour market is a lagging variable normally, but if firms sharply cut hiring and lay off staff, consumption weakens and recession risk rises; the softening so far looks like rebalancing.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: consumer spending number is still tracking around 3% annualized in real term
claims.claim: US consumption was strong in late 2024 (real spending about 3% annualised, strongest services ISM since mid-2022), while manufacturing was weak.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: core pce still about 2.6 2.7% year on year um but if you look at the six Monon annualized it is still tracking lower
claims.claim: Core PCE was about 2.6-2.7% year on year but lower on a six-month annualised basis, so disinflation continued though sticky.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: more aimed at at at stabilizing asset markets and putting a floor over under under under um under asset markets
claims.claim: China's policy measures aimed at stabilising asset markets rather than sustaining a growth rebound.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: there has been a sense of caution you know going into the election so the election could have been a factor that has cause people just to pause for a while
claims.claim: Pre-election caution delayed corporate decisions, so removing uncertainty may release pent-up activity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: you're seeing equities Rising bond yields also Rising which would normally be consistent with kind of a reflationary type scenario
claims.claim: Equities and yields rising together is reflation-like, but oil and copper falling show weak demand, so the move reflects expectations about Trump policy, not current growth.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: higher tariffs would be inflationary obviously it pushes up prices but it is a oneoff effect
claims.claim: Tariffs raise price levels once rather than the inflation rate, so the Fed may look through them if expectations stay anchored.
claims.conditions: if inflation expectations do not shift

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: I think they are more of a bargaining chip as opposed to really the the end game
claims.claim: Tariff bluster may lead to a US-China deal as in 2019-2020.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: I think the interesting thing that that probably the market is jumping on is optimism around supply side policy
claims.claim: Markets are pricing optimism on supply-side policy (tax cuts, deregulation) that raises growth without inflation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: you basically have two years of cart blanch because you've got likely to have the the house and the senate for two years
claims.claim: Republicans control both houses and can use reconciliation for budget measures for two years, though moderates may limit spending and tax cuts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: we've had a decent runup since the FED could by rates by 50 basis points 10 year yields have jumped by I don't know 60 70 basis points
claims.claim: The 10-year yield rose 60-70bp after the Fed's 50bp cut, reflecting deficit concerns.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: the thing that nearly everybody agrees on is the upside risk to bond yields over time and how unsustainable you know the the um trajectory of spending and deficits is in the US
claims.claim: Macro guests agree on upside risk to US yields because deficit trajectory is unsustainable; deficits unlikely to shrink regardless of election winner.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: I've seen Bess saying um you know a strong dollar is is kind of in the US's interests
claims.claim: Bessent as Treasury pick may moderate Trump's weaker-dollar impulse and favour deficit reduction towards 3%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: he sees uh 10-year yields uh surpass or they could surpass 5%
claims.claim: One strategist sees the US 10-year yield possibly surpassing 5%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: bond yields really started to rise on the day pretty much of the 50 basis points cut so it has really been an own goal
claims.claim: Long yields rose from the day of the Fed's 50bp cut, counter to the aim of lowering yields across the curve.
claims.indicator: US long yields vs Fed cut

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: maybe the FED will only CAU every other meeting now and they'll probably stop now at 3 and a half instead of three
claims.claim: JP Morgan revised its Fed path: cuts every other meeting, ending around 3.5%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: I think that it's going to be much harder necessarily to forecast uh just based on kind of godfield and discretion and and reading some uh some economic report as to how the markets will react
claims.claim: With policy uncertainty, forecasting market reactions from discretion or economic reports is harder, favouring systematic strategies.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: equities might end up in one of these kind of parabolic moves to end um possibly end uh this enormously long bull market
claims.claim: The election may trigger a parabolic equity move that ends the long bull market.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: Greenspan kind of made a point that if you can get your the deficit down then that leads a greater backdrop for us to cut rates or keep rates easier
claims.claim: 1990s precedent (Clinton-Greenspan): deficit reduction enabled easier monetary policy; seen as implausible now.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: the challenge with the deficits gets resolved either with some kind of fisical Crisis you know the bond market Vigilantes enforce it or else there's a shift in the the political um leaning on it
claims.claim: Deficits are resolved either by a fiscal crisis enforced by bond vigilantes or a political shift.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: you had all three of the financial sectors turning against you at the same time
claims.claim: October 2024 was the worst month of the year for trend followers because bonds, equities and currencies reversed together.
claims.conditions: when all big sectors reverse at once

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: the US dollar had been uh sold uh against a number of currencies and suddenly it started to strengthen
claims.claim: Fixed income peaked at the Fed cut and sold off, the dollar suddenly strengthened, and equities held, hurting long-bond and short-dollar trend positions.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: it's not unusual in my opinion that you see a big amplitude in performance uh when you have these three sectors moving kind of in the same direction
claims.claim: Large performance swings occur when the three big financial sectors move together, with or against the trend, even for diversified portfolios.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: the middle section kind of medium-term time frames and and here I'm thinking look back did actually even worse than the longer term time frame
claims.claim: Medium-term trend lookbacks did worse than both faster and slower ones in October 2024.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: we did see the bond exposure going from short to long in in around June July late June early July and managers have I think built up a fairly meaningful long exposure going into the FED meeting
claims.claim: Trend managers flipped to long bonds mid-year then got hurt by the post-Fed selloff, and fixed income also drives portfolio correlation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: so the amplitude of the moves has been just long enough and big enough to um to to entice people to switch positions
claims.claim: Bond moves were long enough to flip positions but reversed, creating whipsaw, so fixed income was the swing variable across managers.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: the beta 50 is flat for the month of November it's up 1.91% for the year
claims.claim: Early November 2024: BTOP50 flat (+1.91% YTD), SG CTA -0.78% YTD, SG Trend about -2% YTD, short-term traders -1% in the month; MSCI World +18% YTD.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, MSCI World

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: protection for the first 10 15% decline in the index but but you have full participation in losses Beyond there so you you would still have a big tail risk
claims.claim: Buffer ETFs only protect the first 10-15% of decline, leave a large tail risk and cap upside, so they are not a substitute for bonds.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: had a particular role of stability but also convexity
claims.claim: Bonds provide stability and convexity in a big equity sell-off; trend following or managed futures is the right alternative if rising yields hurt bonds.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: the alternative is uh would just be to shorten the the um duration of bonds
claims.claim: Shortening bond duration (like holding cash) gives income and stability but no convexity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: they're forecasting 3% um annualized uh that's nominal returns for the S&P for the next 10 years that's 1% real um that would put it in the seventh percentile of 10year returns going back to 1930
claims.claim: Goldman forecasts 3% nominal (1% real) annualised S&P 500 returns for the next 10 years, the 7th percentile since 1930, range -1% to +7%.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: they actually think that the equally weighted S&P 500 will outperform by between 2% to 8% annualized
claims.claim: Goldman expects the equal-weighted S&P 500 to outperform the cap-weighted by 2-8% a year, because tech is 30%+ of the index.
claims.direction: long equal weight vs cap weight

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: with 10e yields at about 4% there's quite a good chance that bonds will will outperform equities based on their forecast
claims.claim: With a 4% 10-year yield and a 3% equity forecast, bonds are likely to outperform; expected bond return is the starting yield held to maturity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: when you get this concentration in the NX it tends to be associated with with greater volatility than going forward and it tends to be associated with lower 10-year returns going forward
claims.claim: Historical high index concentration is followed by higher volatility and lower subsequent 10-year returns, since giant firms cannot sustain high earnings growth.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: not only have earnings grown at 7% but you've had you know um lower taxes uh higher sales and and and higher margins all contributing to that and multiples of expanded as well
claims.claim: S&P returns over the past decade came from 7% earnings growth, lower taxes, higher margins and multiple expansion; forecasts depend on margin normalisation and bond yields.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: it feels like with respect to a lot of this technology the winners are priced but not necessarily the impact on the losers
claims.claim: Technology winners are priced in but the damage to losers is not.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: even you know goldin's concentration argument aside if we were into a higher yield environment that in itself would justify lower valuations and reversion to to the mean in terms of valuations
claims.claim: Higher yields would justify lower valuations and below-average returns even apart from concentration.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: nobody said 5 years ago that a small company called Nvidia would suddenly become the the most valuable company
claims.claim: Index leadership changes, so assuming today's top 10 stays top is unreliable; concentration raises volatility but its return effect is unclear.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: as Trend followers we don't need really need to be right about any prediction because we don't make them
claims.claim: Trend followers do not forecast, so they need not be right about forecasts such as Goldman's.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: obviously valuations did jump up over that period from as they say in the report 16 to 22 in terms of PE ratios
claims.claim: Forward PE rose from 16 to 22 over the decade; a further rise to 28 is unlikely but a fall back to 16 is not necessary either.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: if you were to say Trend following if it's a0 four5 sharp if something is running at 12 all with interest rates at 3% you know that's um you know seven or 8% expected returns for Trend following
claims.claim: With Sharpe 0.4-0.5 at 12% vol and 3% cash rates, trend following has about 7-8% expected return, comparing favourably with bonds at 4% and equities at 3% (Goldman).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: it's so hard to sell an alternative product at the moment because the S&P is doing you know 15% per anom and the assumption is it'll continue to do it
claims.claim: Investors extrapolate S&P gains, so alternatives are hard to sell despite diversification logic.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: I think it's 44% of respondents maybe uh using Trend following in in that context which I thought was interesting also ball targeting Frameworks 41%
claims.claim: Invesco 2024 survey: 80% of systematic multi-asset use is factor tilting, 67% asset-class/sector rotation models, 44% trend following, 41% volatility targeting.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: they're saying 90% of uh respondents using AI in some shape or form in their investment process pattern recognition in Market behavior is the most popular use
claims.claim: 90% of Invesco survey respondents use AI, mostly pattern recognition, sentiment analysis (news, earnings calls, Twitter NLP) and real-time position monitoring.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host; caption "Neil Castro blon")
claims.quote: the word systematic is often overlooked and and certainly underappreciated
claims.claim: The core edge is being systematic, doing what the model says, with 50 years of evidence.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne (Dublin-based co-host, macro/systematic investor; caption "alen Don")
claims.quote: there is a Nuance there of when you're you know adding alternative investment strategies to an existing portfolio and those strategies are trading the assets that you already hold
claims.claim: Adding trend to a 60/40 portfolio is not only diversification: trend trades assets already held, so overlap in exposures must be considered in the efficient-frontier analysis.
